question: A 52-year-old man with a history of heavy alcohol use has AST 280 IU/L and ALT 90 IU/L. Which diagnosis does the AST:ALT ratio of >2 most strongly support?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Acute viral hepatitis produces a hepatocellular pattern with ALT typically exceeding AST (ratio <1). An AST:ALT >2 argues strongly against acute viral hepatitis.

Correct. An AST:ALT ratio >2 (here ≈3.1) in a patient with heavy alcohol use is the classic pattern of alcoholic hepatitis. Alcohol preferentially depletes hepatic pyridoxal-5-phosphate, an ALT cofactor, suppressing ALT synthesis relative to AST. A ratio >3 is nearly diagnostic.
Incorrect. NASH typically produces an ALT-predominant or near-equal pattern (AST:ALT ratio ≤1). The high AST:ALT ratio here is more consistent with alcoholic hepatitis.
Incorrect. Autoimmune hepatitis raises aminotransferases in a hepatocellular pattern with ALT usually ≥ AST. An AST:ALT >2 in the context of alcohol use points to alcoholic aetiology.

overallFeedback.feedback: The AST:ALT ratio is a key bedside diagnostic tool: >2 in alcohol users → alcoholic hepatitis; <1 with elevated aminotransferases → viral, NASH, or autoimmune hepatitis. Review the clinical pearl on this ratio.
Well done. AST:ALT >2 in an alcohol user = alcoholic hepatitis until proven otherwise. The mechanism (pyridoxal-5-phosphate depletion suppressing ALT) explains why ALT is disproportionately low.
